the properties of the ordered-defect phases of AB 2 S can be tuned by substitution of cationic components.
the physical properties of ordered-defect phases of AB 2 S4 stoichiometry may be varied by substitution of cations in either the dichalchogenide or the defective layer, or at both sites.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis, structural, magnetic, and electronic properties of the ordered-defect sulphide phases.
the synthesis and characterisation of ordered defect sulphides.
the structure–property relationships in the ordered-defect sulphide phases, with the aim of establishing the role of cation distribution on physical behaviour.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ordered-defect sulphide systems provide an ideal means of studying the interplay of structural and electronic properties in a wide range of materials.
the physical properties of ordered defect phases are determined by the distribution of the constituent ions within the defective layers, with the dichalcogenides providing a passive framework.

the electronic properties of ordered-defect sulphide compounds may be varied systematically through chemical substitution, and that these changes can be rationalised in terms of the cation distribution and the nature of the cation clusters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the electronic properties of ordered-defect chalcogenides can be controlled by a judicious choice of cation distribution, which in turn can be controlled by the choice of chemical substitution.
, for the ordered-defect sulphide phases, the cation distribution may be varied systematically and in a controlled manner by chemical substitution.

the electronic structure of the ordered-defect sulphide phases is strongly dependent on the distribution of the constituent ions, and the latter may be varied in a controlled fashion by chemical substitution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to control the properties of these materials by varying the chemical composition, which can be achieved by substitution.

the structure of ordered-defect sulphide phases can be modified by the substitution of cations in the defective layers and/or in the dichalcogenidic slabs, and this modification can have a dramatic effect on the physical properties of the phases.

ordered-defect structures are a rich playground for the exploration of structure–property relationships, which may be exploited to produce new materials with interesting and potentially useful properties.
